Threat.value: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me

Memory.value: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: I have permanently changed for the worse
My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy

issues.item: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'Hard to Recall Deliberately' conflicts with 'Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.' Deliberate retrieval difficulty and very easy verbal access are opposing states and are hard to reconcile as describing the same patient at the same time, especially alongside 'Overwhelm on Recall,' which implies traumatic recall is effortful and dysregulating rather than easy to discuss.

issues.item: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' directly conflicts with 'When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop.' At this severity level and with strong Trigger↔Memory and Memory→Threat links, these two memory items describe opposing levels of accessibility/distress and are hard to reconcile as the same current presentation.

issues.item: Triggers: Authority Commands: Being given orders or instructions
issues.explanation: The trigger set is hard to reconcile with stalking as the index trauma: 'authority commands' and especially 'bicycle' do not show an evident clinical link to the reported trauma, and the profile provides no memory or appraisal content that would make these idiosyncratic triggers understandable.

Threat items emphasize broad interpersonal attack and generic danger vigilance (loud sounds, scanning exits, watching others for harm), which fits assault/combat/fire trauma better than stalking. For stalking, one would expect threat focused more on being followed, approached, monitored, contacted, or found by the perpetrator.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
issues.explanation: 'I am a weak person' sits awkwardly with this profile and occupation unless supported by appraisal content about failure to protect oneself or family; here the other appraisals center on permanent damage and fear of going crazy, so the weakness item feels less coherent with the stalking-specific formulation than those items.

vignette:
Amir was thirty-four when it began—a slow, creeping presence that he first noticed outside the grocery store near his station. At first, he dismissed it: a man in a dark sedan who seemed to appear wherever Amir went. But over weeks, the sightings became impossible to ignore. The sedan was there when he left the firehouse at odd hours, when he biked home along the river path, when he stopped for coffee. The man never approached, never spoke, but he watched. Amir reported it to the police twice. They found nothing. The stalking lasted four months before the man simply stopped appearing. By then, the damage was done. Amir, now thirty-seven, sat in a therapist’s office with his hands clasped tightly, unable to explain what had happened without feeling his chest tighten and his words dissolve into silence.

The triggers were everywhere. Physical locations—the grocery store, the river path, the corner where the sedan had once idled—could send him reeling. His bicycle, once a source of freedom, now sat untouched in the garage; the sight of it brought the full memory crashing back without warning, a wave of helplessness and fear that left him breathless. When the memory returned, he felt so overwhelmed by emotion that he had to stop whatever he was doing, frozen mid-step. At the firehouse, the sound of the alarm—loud, unexpected—made him flinch and scan for exits, his eyes darting to the doors and windows before he could even register the reason. Amir had come to believe that his reactions proved he was permanently changed for the worse, that the man in the sedan had broken something inside him that could never be repaired. What frightened him most was the thought that he was going crazy—that his hypervigilance, his inability to describe what happened, his constant sense of being watched were signs of unraveling.

Amir watched his colleagues closely, studying their faces for signs of threat, certain that danger could come from anyone. He watched other people too—on the street, in the station, even at home with his wife—looking for the subtle cues that had once been invisible. The more he scanned, the more he found reasons to be alert. A loud noise, a stranger’s prolonged glance, a car that slowed near him: each triggered the memory, and each memory reinforced his belief that he was weak, that a real firefighter would have handled it, would have confronted the man, would not have been reduced to this. The cycle tightened. Because he believed he was weak, he avoided the river path and the grocery store, but those same avoidances made the triggers feel larger, more dangerous. The memory of the sedan idling outside his home returned when he least expected it—in a quiet moment, in a familiar street—and each return deepened his conviction that he had been permanently damaged. He could not find words to describe what happened; the story felt stuck in his throat, a jumble of images and sensations that defied language.

Amir’s wife had noticed. She asked him why he no longer biked, why he flinched at the firehouse alarm, why he checked the locks three times before bed. He told her he was fine. But he was not fine. The threat monitoring had become a constant hum beneath his thoughts: the scanning of exits, the watching of others, the tension in his shoulders at every unexpected sound. The more he monitored, the more he felt he was going crazy, and the more he felt he was going crazy, the more he scanned. His work suffered. He had missed two shifts because he could not bring himself to enter the station after a routine call near the grocery store. His captain had pulled him aside, concerned. Amir had said nothing.

What finally brought him to seek help was a morning in late October. He was driving to work when a black sedan pulled up beside him at a red light. The driver was a stranger—a woman on her phone—but for a split second Amir’s mind went blank with terror. The memory surged, overwhelming, and he pulled over, shaking, unable to continue. He sat on the curb and called his wife. She drove him to the clinic. Now, in the therapist’s office, Amir was terrified that admitting any of this would confirm that he was broken beyond repair. But he was also terrified of staying the same. He wanted to get back on his bicycle. He wanted to stop flinching. He wanted to believe that the man in the sedan had not taken everything.
